results.message: Who was Jesus, to you and your people?

voice_event.speaker: pahc
voice_event.text:
He was a real man, not an idea. Ignatius wrote against people who said Jesus only seemed to be a man, and put it as hard as it can be put: Jesus was truly born, of Mary, from the line of David. He truly ate and drank. He was truly brought before Pilate, truly nailed to the cross, and truly died - not in appearance only, the way those Ignatius wrote against claimed. And Ignatius said he was truly raised, the same way we ourselves will be raised, by the same Father.

When we give thanks over the cup, we call it the vine of David his servant, made known to us through Jesus. More than one of our own households uses those words, not only Ignatius's own. That is the shape of it for us: a real man, really killed, really raised, and now the one through whom we give thanks.

None of us saw him ourselves. What we have is what was handed to us. The apostles preached what they had received from the Lord, and appointed others to carry it forward once they themselves were gone. That chain reached us, household to household, letter by letter - but we will not pretend it was unbroken or that we knew eyewitnesses ourselves. By our own time, that nearness was already something we spoke of as thinning, not something we could simply rely on.

voice_event.speaker: pahc
voice_event.text:
Ignatius calls Jesus Christ our God again and again - in how he opens his letters and in how he closes them. It is not one passing phrase; he reaches for it often. But it is worship, not an argument worked out. How calling Jesus God fits together with calling the Father God - with there being one God - none of us whose writing survives ever wrote out. We can tell you plainly that we called him God. We cannot tell you we had settled how.

Justin, writing to the emperor, says something else that bears here: that God's own Word was present in some measure in every people, so that even a reasonable person born before Christ could in that sense already be called a Christian. He was reaching for something about how Christ relates to God and to all peoples - but again, it is an opening gesture, not a settled answer.

What we gave you at the table was thanksgiving through Jesus to the Father. What we said in worship was that Jesus is God. The worked-out answer to how both those things hold together at once - that belongs to a later world than ours.
